title: Observe Average Teachers, Too
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart borrows writer Alan Moore's advice that aspiring writers should read terrible books, not just great ones, because analyzing failure is often more instructive than admiring excellence — and applies it to classroom observation. He argues teachers should occasionally observe an "average" colleague, not to feel superior, but to build clarity about what ineffective practice looks like and confidence that their own struggles aren't uniquely severe. The piece is explicit about the danger in this practice: approached wrongly, it breeds arrogance or self-righteousness, which Stuart says "warp the soul." Done rightly, observation of an average teacher should still be conducted with honor — noticing strengths as well as weaknesses, and sharing encouragement afterward. Stuart closes by connecting the idea to his own writing career, crediting "bad PD books" with giving him the confidence to write his own.
points: Stuart translates Alan Moore's writing advice (read terrible books, not just great ones) directly into a classroom-observation practice: watching average teachers builds diagnostic clarity that watching only "the best" cannot.
He explicitly warns against the failure mode of this practice — using it to feel superior — framing arrogance and self-righteousness as spiritually corrosive ("they warp the soul").
The piece reframes struggling with one difficult student or class period as a normal, non-unique experience, using observation of peers as evidence against catastrophizing self-talk.
Observing "badly" is repositioned as generative for one's own practice — Stuart credits "terrible PD books" specifically with giving him the confidence to write his own.
quotes: If you are inspired by a good book, there's always the danger of plagiarism, of doing something that is too much like that good book. Whereas, a genuinely helpful reaction to a piece of work that you're reading is, '[My goodness], I could write this [stuff]!'
To me, Moore's advice is super apropos to teachers. Just as Moore advises writers to read terrible books, so, too, should teachers observe average teachers.
The LAST THING that you want in this job is to become arrogant or self-righteous. These states warp the soul. They make you less.
The job, when rightly approached, has a built-in humbling feature. I'm not talking about demeaning yourself when I say "humbling;" I'm talking about taking yourself less seriously.
But sometimes, when you keep struggling day after day with that ONE student or that ONE class period, you can start to think, "Gosh, I'm UNIQUELY lousy at this.

And when you go, do it with honor for the person. Yes, you are going to privately notice in the observation some areas that are not as great as the things you do. But look, too, for areas of strength.
What I hope you take from observing average teachers — what I have taken away, many times — is greater clarity, greater confidence, and greater inspiration for the work tomorrow holds.
